edges.description: Mutant keratins poison the filament network by incorporating into filaments and destabilizing them.

edges.description: Disrupted keratin network renders basal keratinocytes fragile and prone to rupture under mechanical stress.

Cytolysis of the basal keratinocyte is what produces the clinical blister, and is why the cleavage plane is intraepidermal rather than at the dermal-epidermal junction. Every mechanistic route in this entry except the suprabasal desmosomal one reaches the clinical phenotype through this node.
Disrupted hemidesmosome-cytoskeleton linkage leads to skin fragility.

The same plectin loss disrupts the desmin cytoskeleton of skeletal muscle, which is the extracutaneous half of the EBS-MD phenotype and is why that subtype row is the only one in this entry carrying a myopathy.
Thermal breakdown of the mutant filament network is the mechanism behind the seasonal and exertional worsening recorded as a phenotype.
edges.source: Heat Sensitivity of Mutant Keratin Networks

edges.description: Loss of the hemidesmosomal inner plaque leaves basal keratinocytes unable to resist shear, producing the same trauma-induced intraepidermal separation as the keratin and plectin routes.
edges.source: BPAG1-e Deficiency Disrupts the Hemidesmosomal Inner Plaque

edges.description: Reduced keratinocyte adhesion and keratin filament disruption in the lower epidermis converge on the same trauma-induced intraepidermal separation as the structural routes.
edges.source: Exophilin-5 Deficiency Impairs Keratinocyte Vesicle Trafficking and Adhesion

edges.description: Depletion of keratin 14 protein leaves the basal keratin network unable to bear mechanical load, reaching the same cytolysis node as the dominant-negative keratin variants.

edges.description: Suprabasal acantholysis produces superficial erosions and blistering, the shared clinical endpoint with the basal routes even though the cleavage plane differs.

edges.description: Palmoplantar keratoderma is a cardinal feature of the plakophilin route rather than an incidental one, reported in 16 of 18 published biallelic PKP1 cases, so the desmosomal defect reaches this phenotype directly and not only through blistering.

nodes.description: Biallelic DST nonsense variants abolish the epithelial isoform of bullous pemphigoid antigen 1 (BPAG1-e, BP230), the hemidesmosomal inner-plaque protein that anchors keratin intermediate filaments at the basal pole of the keratinocyte. Inner plaques are lost and labelling for plectin, the beta-4 integrin subunit and type XVII collagen is reduced, so the defect destabilizes the wider hemidesmosome rather than one component alone. This is the node the EBS BP230 subtype row acts at.
nodes.id: BPAG1-e Deficiency Disrupts the Hemidesmosomal Inner Plaque

evidence.reference_title: A homozygous nonsense mutation within the dystonin gene coding for the coiled-coil domain of the epithelial isoform of BPAG1 underlies a new subtype of autosomal recessive epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
evidence.snippet: The mutation, p.Gln1124X, leads to the loss of hemidesmosomal inner plaques and a complete absence of skin immunostaining for BPAG1-e, as well as reduced labeling for plectin, the beta4 integrin subunit, and for type XVII collagen.

evidence.reference_title: A homozygous nonsense mutation within the dystonin gene coding for the coiled-coil domain of the epithelial isoform of BPAG1 underlies a new subtype of autosomal recessive epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
evidence.snippet: The 38-year-old affected individual has lifelong generalized trauma-induced spontaneous blisters and erosions, particularly around the ankles.

evidence.reference_title: Loss of desmoplakin tail causes lethal acantholytic epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence.snippet: Aberrant mRNA transcripts that predict premature termination of translation with loss of the three intermediate filament-binding subdomains in the DP tail were detected by RT-PCR.

evidence.reference_title: Novel truncating mutations in PKP1 and DSP cause similar skin phenotypes in two Brazilian families.
evidence.snippet: Loss-of-function mutations in the DSP gene can result in a phenotype similar to ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome resulting from PKP1 mutations but only DSP pathology is associated with cardiac disease.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex.

nodes.description: The two suprabasal routes in this entry. Loss of plakophilin 1, a desmosomal plaque protein expressed mainly in the spinous layer, or truncation of the desmoplakin tail that carries desmoplakin's intermediate filament-binding subdomains, detaches keratin filaments from desmosomes above the basal layer. The cleavage plane is therefore suprabasal rather than intrabasal, and the histology is acantholysis resembling pemphigus rather than basal-cell cytolysis. This node is drawn separately from the basal routes for that reason, and is where the EBS-PD and LAEB subtype rows act.
nodes.id: Desmosomal Plaque Deficiency Causes Suprabasal Acantholysis

evidence.reference_title: Loss of desmoplakin tail causes lethal acantholytic epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence.snippet: Histology showed suprabasal clefting and acantholysis throughout the spinous layer, mimicking pemphigus. Electron microscopy revealed disconnection of keratin intermediate filaments from desmosomes.

evidence.reference_title: Ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome: Two new cases and review of this desmosomal genodermatosis.
evidence.snippet: One specific component of desmosomes is plakophilin 1 (PKP1), which is mainly expressed in the spinous layer of the epidermis. Loss-of-function autosomal recessive mutations in PKP1 result in ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility (EDSF) syndrome

evidence.reference_title: Ectodermal dysplasia-skin fragility syndrome: Two new cases and review of this desmosomal genodermatosis.
evidence.snippet: Skin fragility and nail involvement were present in all affected individuals (18/18), with most cases showing palmoplantar keratoderma (16/18), alopecia/hypotrichosis (16/18) and perioral fissuring/cheilitis (12/15; not commented on in 3 cases).

nodes.description: Mutant keratins exert a dominant-negative effect by incorporating into keratin filaments and poisoning the entire filament network. This disrupts filament architecture and leads to keratin aggregate formation, particularly under conditions of mechanical or thermal stress.

evidence.reference_title: Defining keratin protein function in skin epithelia: epidermolysis bullosa simplex and its aftermath.
evidence.snippet: Defects in K5-K14 filament network architecture cause basal keratinocytes to become fragile, and account for their rupture upon exposure to mechanical trauma

evidence.reference_title: Keratins as an Inflammation Trigger Point in Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex.
evidence.snippet: Keratin aggregates display impaired dynamics of assembly and diminished solubility and appear to be the trigger for endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress upon being phosphorylated by MAPKs

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex.
evidence.snippet: biallelic pathogenic variants in CD151, DST, or EXPH5

nodes.description: Biallelic EXPH5 truncating variants remove the C-terminus of exophilin-5 (Slac2-b), a Rab27B effector in intracellular vesicle trafficking. The product is not a structural component of the keratin-hemidesmosome apparatus, as the keratin, plectin and BPAG1-e routes' products are; the route to fragility runs instead through disordered vesicle handling, with perinuclear and plasma-membrane-proximal vesicle accumulation, keratin filament disruption and reduced keratinocyte adhesion in the lower epidermis. This is the node the EBS EXPH5 subtype row acts at.
nodes.id: Exophilin-5 Deficiency Impairs Keratinocyte Vesicle Trafficking and Adhesion

evidence.reference_title: Germline Mutation in EXPH5 Implicates the Rab27B Effector Protein Slac2-b in Inherited Skin Fragility.
evidence.snippet: Analysis of an affected person's skin showed loss of Slac2-b immunostaining (C-terminal antibody), disruption of keratinocyte adhesion within the lower epidermis, and an increased number of perinuclear vesicles.

evidence.reference_title: Germline Mutation in EXPH5 Implicates the Rab27B Effector Protein Slac2-b in Inherited Skin Fragility.
evidence.snippet: A role for Slac2-b in keratinocyte biology was supported by findings of cytoskeletal disruption (mainly keratin intermediate filaments) and decreased keratinocyte adhesion in both keratinocytes from an affected subject and after shRNA knockdown of Slac2-b in normal keratinocytes.

nodes.description: Mutant keratin filament networks are thermally unstable. Elevated temperature causes filament breakdown into aggregates, explaining the clinical observation that blistering worsens in warm weather and with increased perspiration. This is particularly prominent in localized EBS.
nodes.id: Heat Sensitivity of Mutant Keratin Networks

evidence.reference_title: Temperature sensitivity of the keratin cytoskeleton and delayed spreading of keratinocyte lines derived from EBS patients.
evidence.snippet: after thermal stress a reduced stability of the keratin filaments was demonstrable in the epidermolysis bullosa simplex cell lines, with filaments breaking into aggregates

nodes.description: Worsening of blistering during warm weather or with increased physical activity and perspiration. Caused by thermal instability of mutant keratin filament networks. Particularly prominent in localized EBS affecting hands and feet.

evidence.reference_title: Temperature sensitivity of the keratin cytoskeleton and delayed spreading of keratinocyte lines derived from EBS patients.

evidence.reference_title: Stabilizing mutations of KLHL24 ubiquitin ligase cause loss of keratin 14 and human skin fragility.
evidence.snippet: We have identified start-codon mutations in the KLHL24 gene in five patients with EB.

evidence.reference_title: Monoallelic Mutations in the Translation Initiation Codon of KLHL24 Cause Skin Fragility.
evidence.snippet: monoallelic mutations, c.1A>G and c.2T>C, in the translation initiation codon of the gene encoding kelch-like protein 24 (KLHL24) in 14 individuals with a distinct skin-fragility phenotype and skin cleavage within basal keratinocytes

nodes.description: Heterozygous start-codon variants in KLHL24 produce a receptor lacking its first 28 residues, which can no longer autoubiquitinate and therefore accumulates. Keratin 14 is a substrate of this receptor, so the stabilized form drives excessive ubiquitination and degradation of keratin 14. The basal keratin network is depleted without any mutation in a keratin gene, which is why this node is drawn separately from the dominant-negative route. This is the node the EBS KLHL24 subtype row acts at.
nodes.id: KLHL24 Gain-of-Function Drives Ubiquitin-Mediated Keratin 14 Degradation

evidence.reference_title: Stabilizing mutations of KLHL24 ubiquitin ligase cause loss of keratin 14 and human skin fragility.
evidence.snippet: We have further identified keratin 14 (KRT14) as a KLHL24 substrate and found that KLHL24-ΔN28 induces excessive ubiquitination and degradation of KRT14.

evidence.reference_title: Stabilizing mutations of KLHL24 ubiquitin ligase cause loss of keratin 14 and human skin fragility.
evidence.snippet: Using a knock-in mouse model, we have confirmed that the Klhl24 mutations lead to stabilized Klhl24-ΔN28 and cause Krt14 degradation.

evidence.reference_title: Defining keratin protein function in skin epithelia: epidermolysis bullosa simplex and its aftermath.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex: recurrent and de novo mutations in the KRT5 and KRT14 genes, phenotype/genotype correlations, and implications for genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis.

Keratins 5 and 14 are the obligate type II and type I intermediate filament partners that copolymerize to form the 10 nm filament network providing mechanical resilience to basal keratinocytes.

evidence.reference_title: Defining keratin protein function in skin epithelia: epidermolysis bullosa simplex and its aftermath.
evidence.snippet: Most cases of EBS are due to dominantly acting mutations in keratin 14 (K14) or K5, the type I and II intermediate filament (IF) proteins that copolymerize to form a pancytoplasmic network of 10 nm filaments in basal keratinocytes of epidermis and related epithelia

evidence.reference_title: Keratins and epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

nodes.description: Basal keratinocytes with disrupted keratin networks rupture (cytolyse) when subjected to mechanical trauma. The blistering in EBS is intraepidermal, occurring within the basal cell layer rather than at tissue interfaces, distinguishing it from junctional and dystrophic EB.

nodes.description: Progressive muscular dystrophy in EBS with muscular dystrophy (EBS-MD) caused by PLEC mutations. Plectin is essential for muscle cytoskeletal integrity. Skeletal muscle biopsies show dystrophic features with variation in fiber size, degenerative myofibrillar changes, and pathological desmin-positive protein aggregates.

evidence.snippet: The most common disorder is autosomal recessive disease epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy (EBS-MD), which is characterized by skin blistering and progressive muscle weakness

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex: recurrent and de novo mutations in the KRT5 and KRT14 genes, phenotype/genotype correlations, and implications for genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis.

nodes.description: Mutations in PLEC disrupt plectin, a giant cytoskeletal crosslinker that connects the keratin intermediate filament network to hemidesmosomes at the dermal-epidermal junction and to the desmin cytoskeleton in muscle. Loss of plectin causes a dual phenotype affecting both skin (blistering) and skeletal muscle (progressive dystrophy).

evidence.reference_title: Muscle-Related Plectinopathies.

evidence.reference_title: Plectin-related skin diseases.
evidence.snippet: Plectin deficiency causes autosomal recessive epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) with involvement of the skin and other organs, such as muscle and gastrointestinal tract, depending on the expression pattern of the defective protein

nodes.description: Thickening of the skin on palms and soles, particularly prominent in EBS severe (Dowling-Meara) subtype. May develop progressively with age.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex.
evidence.snippet: Additional features can include hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles (keratoderma), nail dystrophy, milia, and hyper- and/or hypopigmentation

nodes.description: Intraepidermal blistering caused by basal keratinocyte fragility. Blisters arise at sites of mechanical trauma and generally heal without significant scarring, distinguishing EBS from dystrophic EB.

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex.
evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is characterized by fragility of the skin (and mucosal epithelia in some instances) that results in non-scarring blisters and erosions caused by minor mechanical trauma

evidence.reference_title: Epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence.snippet: Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is an inherited, heterogeneous group of rare genetic dermatoses characterized by mucocutaneous fragility and blister formation, inducible by often minimal trauma
